01 · Overview

A savings feature that existed
but didn't work

UKRSIBBANK's mobile app already had a feature called "Дрімка" (Dream) — a savings jar where users could set aside money toward a personal goal. On paper it solved a real need. In practice, almost no one used it.

The feature lacked clarity, motivation mechanics, and any meaningful UX logic. Users couldn't understand how to deposit, track progress, or withdraw. The product wasn't broken — it was invisible.

My task: rethink the savings experience from the ground up, validate new hypotheses through research, and ship a redesigned feature — now called "Safe" (Сейф) — that actually drives behavior change.

02 · Process

How we approached it

We ran a parallel, multi-stream research process. No single method gave us the full picture — so we used three together and synthesized the findings into a unified opportunity space.

Step 01

Kickoff & Alignment

Defined the product problem, business goals, success metrics, user groups, and research constraints. Mapped competitive landscape — Monobank, PrivatBank, Sense Bank — to understand the existing savings patterns in Ukrainian banking.

Step 02

DRMSA Analysis

Audited the existing "Дрімка" feature: flows, drop-offs, unclear labels, missing affordances. Identified 8 key opportunity areas across access, motivation, terminology, and gamification.

Step 03

User Research

Conducted in-depth interviews using the Interview Arc method. Explored past savings behavior, emotional triggers, mental models around "jars," and unmet needs. Built individual CJMs per user, then merged into a master journey.

Step 04

Synthesis & Prioritization

Affinity mapped all findings. Ran Impact/Effort scoring to prioritize hypotheses. Co-designed solutions with the team and moved into prototyping and validation.

03 · Kickoff

Setting the foundation

Before any research started, the team aligned on what we were actually trying to solve. The kickoff session defined the product goal (increase meaningful savings engagement), business metrics, target user segments, research constraints, and a competitive snapshot.

We mapped out Monobank's "Banks," PrivatBank's savings tools, and Sense Bank's approach — not to copy them, but to understand what mental models Ukrainian users already had around digital savings jars.

Kickoff session: product definition, research plan, competitive analysis, and team alignment

04 · User Research

Talking to real savers

We structured interviews using the Interview Arc method — a progressive script that moves from warm-up through pre-experience, into the main theme, and post-experience reflection. This helped us understand not just what users want, but why they save, when they fail, and what keeps them motivated.

"I want to save for a car, but every time I look at the app I forget the feature even exists. I end up just using a separate cash envelope at home."

— Interview participant, retail banking user

Interview Arc structure · Pre Experience → Main Theme → Post Experience · question prioritization

What we explored

Past savings behavior and mental models · What tools users currently use (physical envelopes, separate accounts, other bank apps) · Emotional triggers — what motivates someone to start saving · Pain points when saving falls apart · Whether users had ever used digital savings tools in banking apps · Attitude toward shared savings goals

Key signals from interviews

Visibility is everything. Users forget features exist if they're buried. Goal clarity motivates. A named, visual jar with a target amount creates a psychological commitment device. Automation removes friction. Manual top-ups fail; users want to "set and forget." Shared savings emerged as an unexpected strong desire — saving together with a partner or family.

05 · Customer Journey Map

Mapping the full savings journey

For each research participant, we built an individual CJM — capturing their actions, thoughts, emotions, and pain points across 8 phases: from choosing a savings tool, through opening a "jar," setting goals, depositing, tracking progress, and eventually withdrawing or closing.

Individual maps were then merged into one master CJM, giving us a unified view of where the current experience broke down and where the greatest opportunities lived.

Master CJM · 8 journey phases · Actions → Thoughts → Emotions → Pain Points → Opportunities

06 · Synthesis

From raw data to opportunity themes

After interviews, we affinity-mapped all findings across 8 core themes. Each sticky note was a real user quote or observation — grouped by pattern, not by assumption. This surfaced what users actually struggled with, not what we thought they did.

Affinity map · 8 opportunity themes across 5 journey phases

Theme 01 · Access

Users couldn't find the feature — navigation to "Дрімка" was buried under account settings with no visible entry from the home screen.

Theme 02 · Onboarding hints

First-time users didn't understand what a "Дрімка" was — the name was abstract and there was no explanation of how it worked.

Theme 03 · Goal creation

Opening a savings jar was too many steps — users dropped off before completing setup because the flow felt like opening a bank account.

Theme 05 · Top-up & accumulation

Manual deposits fail. Users wanted automatic regular contributions — the same way they think about utility bills, not active decisions.

Theme 06 · Motivation

Progress visualization and gamification mechanics (streaks, milestones, celebrations) significantly increased reported likelihood to continue saving.

Theme — Competitive insight

Monobank's "Banks" (Банки) with shared savings and visual goal images were cited as a reference for what "feels right" — we took notes.

07 · Prioritization

What to build first

With a long list of opportunities, we needed to decide what would ship in the first version. We ran an Impact/Effort matrix — scoring each hypothesis by its user impact (1–10) against implementation complexity. This gave the product team a shared, defensible prioritization framework.

The matrix revealed a clear cluster of high-impact, reasonable-effort improvements: visual goal naming, automatic top-ups, shared savings jars, and home screen visibility. These became the core of v1.

Impact vs. Implementation Effort matrix · each card = a validated hypothesis from research

08 · Before & After

From "Дрімка" to "Safe"

The original "Дрімка" screen was functional at best. It used abstract terminology, lacked visual goal-setting, had no progress indicators, and offered no path to automatic contributions. The redesigned "Safe" (Сейф) reframes the entire mental model — from a forgotten banking feature to a personal financial commitment device.

Before · Дрімка
After · Safe (Сейф)

Left: original "Dream Jar" confirmation · Right: redesigned "Safe" success state with clearer CTA hierarchy

What changed

Naming: "Дрімка" → "Safe" — concrete, universally understood, carries a sense of security and intentionality.

Visuals: Goal image (e.g. car photo) replaces abstract icon — creates personal attachment to the savings goal.

Success state: Celebratory confirmation screen reinforces the behavior with positive feedback immediately after setup.

Key new features shipped

Automatic regular top-ups — set frequency, amount, and date once, done.

Shared savings — invite family or a partner to contribute to the same Safe together.

Goal visualization — photo, target amount, and progress bar always visible.

Streamlined setup — reduced from 9+ steps to 4 core actions.

10 · Outcomes & Learnings

What this project taught me

This was one of the most research-heavy projects I've worked on — and also one where research directly shaped every design decision. The original "Дрімка" wasn't a bad idea; it just never listened to users.

The biggest lesson: visibility and naming are not cosmetic decisions. Renaming the feature and surfacing it from the home screen — changes that sound trivial — had more projected impact than any new interaction pattern we designed.

The project also reinforced the value of the Impact/Effort matrix as a communication tool, not just a prioritization tool. It gave the product and engineering teams a shared language for trade-offs, and made design decisions feel evidence-based rather than opinionated.

"Naming
is UX"
Switching from "Дрімка" (abstract/playful) to "Safe" (concrete/trustworthy) reduced onboarding confusion significantly in testing
Auto >
Manual
Every user who dropped off did so during manual deposit flows. Automatic contributions were the single highest-impact change we shipped
Shared
saves more
Shared savings jars emerged as an unprompted desire in 70%+ of interviews — a feature not in the original brief that made it into v1
